patients.label: 44-year-old woman with ovarian and endometrial cancer who developed gingival inflammation during bevacizumab chemotherapy
attribution_limitations: The third course is called a docetaxel and carboplatin combination, while the regimen of paclitaxel and carboplatin is described as repeated six times; the source does not say whether paclitaxel was replaced by docetaxel in the third course.
The "first injection" of the adverse-effect sentence does not name the drug; bevacizumab was first given with the second course, so the anchor could be a chemotherapy or a bevacizumab injection.

The first dental clinic visit in the opening sentence and the first dental office visit on the day of the 11th course are presumably the same visit but the source does not say so; they are kept as separate events without an ordering relation.

The authors assert without hedging that bevacizumab induced the gingival inflammation ("certainly induced"; "induced by administration of bevacizumab"), recorded as a bevacizumab adverse effect. The same report states that poor oral hygiene made the symptoms worse and that the patient was told the symptoms derived from insufficient cleaning and oral contamination as well as the chemotherapy itself; the plaque-plus-mucositis synergy is only hedged ("It is possible").
The anchor of "1 year later" for the CEA value returning to the reference range is not named in the sentence; it follows an increase after the 18th course.
The CA19-9 reference interval is printed with the label "CA19-1" in the source (print artefact); it is read as the CA19-9 interval because the same sentence names CA19-9 and CA125.
The hemorrhage is called "serious" in the Figure 1 caption and "serous" in the text and Figure 2 caption; treated as a print variation.

Bevacizumab-alone counts do not reconcile arithmetically: an additional 16 injections after the second to sixth course (21 prescriptions in total), the 11th course called the sixth course of only bevacizumab, an additional 10 courses after the first dental visit, and the 21st course printed as the last administration. Arithmetic-only mismatch, not a source conflict.

"Complete tolerance of inflammation" after several additional weeks from the end of chemotherapy is unclear wording; the sentence does not say when or whether complete resolution was documented, and Figure 2 at 4 weeks still shows edematous gingiva with serous hemorrhage. The conclusion only states in general terms that the adverse effect disappears after chemotherapy.

The end-tuft brush is described as "for implanted teeth", which suggests dental implants, but the source never states that the patient has implants (the examination lists 28 teeth and 16 filled teeth).
